This writ petition instituted in the year 2023, questions the land acquisition proceedings carried out in the year 1956.

The petitioner s/o Sh. Munsi Ram, seeks:-
(a). declaration that the acquisition of land bearing Khasra No.344/317 measuring 00-09-00 Bighas situated in Hadbast No.96, Khata Khatuni No.20/21, Mohal Gural,
Tehsil Dalhousie, District Chamba, on the basis of notification issued in August 1956,
is unconstitutional, on the ground that the same had lapsed.
Whether reporters of Local Papers may be allowed to see the judgment?

Yes (b) writ of mandamus to the respondents-State to work in accordance with law by following the procedure mandated .
under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (for brevity '2013 Act'), for acquring the above described land.

sentences.text: Petitioner has no cause of action in his favour.
He has suppressed material facts in the petition.
Petitioner's claim against 'the 1956 acquisition of land' is otherwise barred by limitation and suffers from delay and laches.
Land in question was acquired by the State in accordance with law in the year 1956.
Compensation due and admissible was paid to the landowners in accordance with law.

After the .
acquisition of land, mutation was required to be attested, which somehow could not be attested.
It was entered and attested on 17.05.2023.
Petitioner has no right over Khasra No.344/317.
Respondents are owners of the land by way of acquisition.
No right of the petitioner much less constitutional right has been violated by the respondents.
Petitioner is not in possession of the land.

Award in this regard was passed by the Land Acquisition Collector on 23.08.1956.

The acquired land viz Khasra No.8/10 & 317 was owned by 12 different landowners.

Petitioner's .

During process of payment of compensation, the notices were issued not only to landowners but to petitioner's father as well.

Petitioner's father, Sh. Munsi Ram-the tenant over the land, made a statement before the Land Acquisition Collector that he would have no objection in case the entire compensation qua Khasra No.317, which was put to acquisition by the State and was co-owned by Bhagat Ram and other landowners, is actually paid to its landowners.
Along with compliance affidavit, the respondents have also placed on record the aforesaid statement made by petitioner's father in the year 1956.

The compliance affidavit further goes on to state that on the basis of award passed by Land Acquisition Collector, the compensation amount was calculated and was paid to the original owners of the land.
Out of 12 landowners, 6 received the amount of compensation in terms of their share.
Notices were issued to remaining landowners including one Sh. Bhagat Ram.

The remaining landowners did not turn up to receive the amount of compensation .
falling to their shares.
Consequently, the Land Acquisition Collector deposited the balance amount of compensation in the Government Treasury on 27.11.1963.

Along with the compliance affidavit,
the notices dated 20.02.1957 issued to the landowners and certain other documents, reflecting deposit of balance amount of compensation falling to the share of remaining landowners, have been appended.
Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the amount due to Sh. Bhagat Ram, one of the landowners of Khasra No.317, was not actually paid to him.
The respondent-State did not complete the acquisition proceedings.
The possession of the property was not taken over by State.

Hence, Sh.
Munsi Ram and thereafter, his successor-in-interest, i.e. the present petitioner, became the owner of the land in question.
Petitioner's possession over the land in question till date has not been disturbed.

Therefore, in light of Section 24 of the 2013 Act, the land acquisition proceedings, if any, undertaken by the respondent-State in the year 1957 shall be deemed to have lapsed and the respondent-State is required to de novo start the land acquisition proceedings in accordance with the Act .

The above contentions are misdirected:-
5(iii)(a).
In view of the admitted factual position, firslty, the petitioner has no locus standi to seek the reliefs prayed for by him in the writ petition.
It is not in dispute that the petitioner's father was not the landowner over Khasra No.317 in 1956, when the land was acquired by the State.

Admittedly, petitioner's father had unambiguously stated before the Land Acquisition Collector that he had no right in the price/compensation of land, which he was cultivating as a tenant; That price/compensation of the land should be given to landowners-Bhagat Ram etc.
It is the stand of the respondents-State that compensation thereafter was paid to six landowners and deposited for the remaining six landowners, in accordance with law.

The landowners have not raised any dispute on any of the related points, i.e. on compensation .
having not been paid to them or less compensation paid to them or compensation amount having not been deposited in accordance with law or possession of the acquired land not taken from them etc. r to

The afore being the position and facts pleaded in the compliance affidavit dated 26.04.2024 having not been disputed by the petitioner, it is not understandable as to in which capacity, the petitioner is seeking the relief to declare the acquisition process of 1956 as having lapsed.
He has no locus standi to seek such relief.
5(iii)(b).
Secondly, petitioner's claim made in the year 2023 in the instant writ petition for declaring the 1956 acquisition of land as lapsed otherwise also suffers from unexplained huge delay and laches.
Such a relief as claimed, in view of facts emerging from the case file cannot be granted in this writ petition.
5(iii)(c).

Thirdly, claim of deemed lapsing of the 1956 acquisition of land and requirement of de novo land .
acquisition as per Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act can also not be accepted.

Section 24 of 2013 Act reads as under:-

sentences.text: Firstly, as discussed earlier, the petitioner has no locus standi to institute the writ petition for seeking the reliefs prayed for by him, more so in light of facts as have come on record; He being the successor in interest of Sh. Munsi Ram, and Sh. Munsi Ram the recorded tenant on the land having given a statement before the Land Acquisition Collector that entire assessed compensation amount in terms of the Award dated 23.08.1956 be paid to the landowners.
These facts have not been disputed by the petitioner.

Secondly, petitioner's contention is that under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, if any one of the two ingredients was attracted, i.e. either the physical possession of the land was not taken or the compensation was not paid as the case may .
be, the acquisition proceedings would be deemed to have lapsed.
However, in Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal and Ors.1, Hon'ble Apex Court has held that land acquisition proceedings lapse only when twin conditions are met, i.e. non- payment of compensation to the landowners together with failure of the State to take physical possession of the acquired land and not otherwise.

sentences.text: (a) in case the award is not made as on 1- 1-2014, the date of commencement of the 2013 Act, there is no lapse of proceedings.
Compensation has to be determined under the provisions of the 2013 Act.

In case the award has been passed within the window period of five years excluding the period covered by an interim order of the court, then proceedings shall continue as provided under Section 24(1)(b) of the 2013 Act under the 1894 Act as if it has not been repealed.
The word 'or' used in Section 24(2) between possession and compensation has to be read as 'nor' or as 'and'.

The deemed lapse of land acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act takes place where due to inaction of authorities for five years or more prior to commencement of the said Act, the possession of land has not been taken nor compensation has been paid.
In other words, in case possession has been taken, compensation has not been paid then there is no lapse.
Similarly, if compensation has been paid, possession has not been taken then there is no lapse.
The expression 'paid' in the main part of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act does not include a deposit of compensation in court.

The consequence of non-deposit is provided in the proviso to Section 24(2) in case it has not been deposited with respect to majority of landholdings then all beneficiaries (landowners) as on the date of notification for land acquisition under Section 4 of the .
1894 Act
shall be entitled to compensation in accordance with the provisions of the 2013 Act.

In case the obligation under Section 31 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 has not been fulfilled,
interest under Section 34 of the said Act can be granted.

Non -deposit of compensation (in court)
does not result in the lapse of land acquisition proceedings.

In case of non-deposit with respect to the majority of holdings for five years or more, compensation under the 2013 Act has to be paid to the 'landowners' as on the date of notification for land acquisition under Section 4 of the 1894 Act.

In case a person has been tendered the compensation as provided under Section 31(1) of the 1894 Act, it is not open to him to claim that acquisition has lapsed under Section 24(2) due to non-payment or non- deposit of compensation in court.
The obligation to pay is complete by tendering the amount under Section 31(1).

The landowners who had refused to accept compensation or who sought reference for higher compensation, cannot claim that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed under Section 24(2)
of the 2013 Act.
The proviso to Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act is to be treated as part of Section 24(2), not part of Section 24(1)(b).

The mode of taking possession under the 1894 Act and as contemplated under Section 24(2)
is by drawing of inquest report/memorandum.

Once award .
has been passed on taking possession under Section 16 of the 1894 Act, the land vests in State there is no divesting provided under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, as once possession has been taken Ramesh Kumar vs State Of H.P. & Ors on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/54259785/
9 there is no lapse under Section 24(2).

In the instant case, the landlords to whose r favour to whom compensation had either been paid or in the compensation had been deposited by the State in terms of the 1956 award, have not questioned the acquisition proceedings on any point, that may be available to them, be it on account of payment of compensation to them or involving possession of the land etc.

That being the position,
it cannot be held that 1956 land acquisition proceedings are to be deemed to have lapsed or that fresh acquisition proceedings for the land are required to be conducted under the 2013 Act.
Thirdly, the respondents have disputed petitioner's allegations of his being in continuous possession of the land in question.

However, even if the petitioner is assumed to be in possession of .
the land at present, in view of admitted facts, prima facie, nature of his such possession can only be termed as that of an encroacher.
In any case in the given facts, he cannot be permitted to setup the reliefs as claimed in the writ petition.

Fourthly,
 r to  the acquisition proceedings completed in the year 1956.
These proceedings were cannot be allowed to be questioned in the year 2023.

Petitioner's father, Sh. Munsi Ram-the tenant, over the land had admittedly not objected to the acquisition proceedings at the relevant time and payment of compensation amount in favour of the landowners.

His son-petitioner cannot be heard to complain that since some of the landowners were allegedly not paid the compensation amount, in accordance with law, therefore, land acquisition proceedings are to be deemed to have lapsed or that subsequently, he became owner of the land and therefore, land acquisition proceedings that culminated decades prior to that are to be assumed to be vitiated.

In .
case, petitioner has any dispute on facts, then it is for him to take appropriate remedy in accordance with law for proving such facts to claim reliefs as may be admissible to him in law.

Conclusion.
The concern, if any, with the above issues is that of the landowners.

Petitioner has no right to claim the .
reliefs prayed in the writ petition.

Merely, because of petitioner's assertion that with afflux of time,
he has allegedly now assumed the status of landowner, will not entitle him to turn the clock backward to the year 1956 and then claim that he has a right over the land and on that basis can seek the reliefs, as set forth in the petition instituted in the year 2023.
5(iv)(c).

Petitioner's claim that 1956 land acquisitio n proceedings be declared as having lapsed and for fresh acquisition in accordance with Section 24 of the 2013 Act suffers from decades of unexplained delay and laches.
5(iv)(d).

In the given facts of the case, as have come out from the record, which are not in dispute, it cannot be held that 1956 land acquisition proceedings are deemed to have lapsed thereby requiring fresh acquisition proceedings in view of Section 24 of the 2013 Act.
In view of above discussion, more particularly in para 5, the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner cannot be granted to him.
This writ petition is therefore, dismissed.
Pending miscellaneous application(s), if any, also stands disposed of.

Therefore, in light of Section 24 of the 2013 Act, the land acquisition proceedings, if any, undertaken by the respondent-State in the year 1957 shall be deemed to have lapsed and the respondent-State is required to de novo start the land acquisition proceedings in accordance with the Act .
He has no locus standi to seek such relief.
Secondly, petitioner's claim made in the year 2023 in the instant writ petition for declaring the 1956 acquisition of land as lapsed otherwise also suffers from unexplained huge delay and laches.
Such a relief as claimed, in view of facts emerging from the case file cannot be granted in this writ petition.

Compensation has to be determined under the provisions of the 2013 Act.
In case the award has been passed within the window period of five years excluding the period covered by an interim order of the court, then proceedings shall continue as provided under Section 24(1)(b) of the 2013 Act under the 1894 Act as if it has not been repealed.
The word 'or' used in Section 24(2) between possession and compensation has to be read as 'nor' or as 'and'.
The deemed lapse of land acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act takes place where due to inaction of authorities for five years or more prior to commencement of the said Act, the possession of land has not been taken nor compensation has been paid.
The landowners who had refused to accept compensation or who sought reference for higher compensation, cannot claim that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed under Section 24(2)
of the 2013 Act.
That being the position,
it cannot be held that 1956 land acquisition proceedings are to be deemed to have lapsed or that fresh acquisition proceedings for the land are required to be conducted under the 2013 Act.
Thirdly, the respondents have disputed petitioner's allegations of his being in continuous possession of the land in question.
However, even if the petitioner is assumed to be in possession of .
the land at present, in view of admitted facts, prima facie, nature of his such possession can only be termed as that of an encroacher.
His son-petitioner cannot be heard to complain that since some of the landowners were allegedly not paid the compensation amount, in accordance with law, therefore, land acquisition proceedings are to be deemed to have lapsed or that subsequently, he became owner of the land and therefore, land acquisition proceedings that culminated decades prior to that are to be assumed to be vitiated.
Petitioner's father-a tenant over the land in question, having forfeited his right in the year 1956 to receive payment of compensation in lieu of acquisition of land, in favour of the landowners,
there is no vested right in the petitioner now:- to demand compensation in lieu of land acquisition;
to seek declaration that land acquisition under the 1956 acquisition proceedings are to be deemed to have lapsed; to claim de novo acquisition of land in accordance with Section 24 of the 2013 Act.
Petitioner's claim that 1956 land acquisitio n proceedings be declared as having lapsed and for fresh acquisition in accordance with Section 24 of the 2013 Act suffers from decades of unexplained delay and laches.

Secondly, petitioner's contention is that under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, if any one of the two ingredients was attracted, i.e. either the physical possession of the land was not taken or the compensation was not paid as the case may .
be, the acquisition proceedings would be deemed to have lapsed.
However, in Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal and Ors.1, Hon'ble Apex Court has held that land acquisition proceedings lapse only when twin conditions are met, i.e. non- payment of compensation to the landowners together with failure of the State to take physical possession of the acquired land and not otherwise.
